title: A Father's Warning, a Son's March
story:
The great sacrifice of Kashyapa had ended, and the gods and the Asuras had returned to their own worlds. All of them, that is, except one — and Vajranabha had not gone home to rest. He had gone home to prepare for war.

The lord of the unbreachable city Vajra had decided that the three worlds belonged to him, and he came to his father Kashyapa to set the conquest in motion, expecting perhaps a blessing. He received a warning instead.

"Sakra is the eldest of you all," said Kashyapa, "and the foremost in accomplishments. He is endued with great ascetic power, strong by nature, devoted to the Brahmanas, grateful, the king of the whole world and the refuge of the good and the pious. He holds his sovereignty because he works for the well-being of all creatures. You will not be able to vanquish him, Vajranabha — you yourself will be killed. As a man who rouses the anger of a serpent meets his own destruction, so you will be destroyed in no time."

Vajranabha heard the words as a man hears medicine when he is already in love with death: as one whose limbs are bound by the noose of Death refuses the remedy, so the king of the Asuras refused his father's counsel. He saluted Kashyapa, turned away, and began to gather his kinsmen, his warriors, his friends. He would conquer the three worlds — and he would begin with the region of the celestials.

But the gods were already ahead of him. Indra and Upendra had sent the swans, the celestial birds who are brothers of the gods, begotten by Kashyapa, to bring about Vajranabha's destruction; and when the swans carried word that the Asura was marching on heaven, the Yadavas held a worried council. "Vajranabha will be killed by Pradyumna," they said. "But Vajranabha's daughter and the daughters of Sunabha are the devoted wives of our heroes, and they are all with child, their time near at hand. What are we to do?"

They sent the swans back to Indra and Krishna with the question, and the gods answered with a promise: "Do not fear. You will have beautiful sons, like Kama himself in accomplishments — even in the womb they will master the Vedas with their auxiliaries. Your sons will grow to youth at once, and they will be masters of every future topic and every scripture."

The swans carried the promise to the city of Vajra, where the Yadava heroes waited with their wives. Prabhavati bore Pradyumna a son, omniscient and youthful like his father; after a month Chandravati bore Chandraprabha, who resembled Gada; and Gunavati bore Gunavan — all of them youthful, omniscient, wonderful. The boys mastered every shastra as they grew, and they moved freely about the turrets of the palaces, shown to the Daityas, the text says, by the very desire of Indra and Upendra.

The Daityas stationed in the sky saw them and carried the news at once to Vajranabha, who was making ready to conquer heaven. "Arrest them!" cried the irrepressible king of the Asuras. "They have trespassed into my house!" Soldiers ringed the quarters, and cries arose on every side: "Seize them, kill them!" The mothers, who loved their sons, began to weep.

Pradyumna stood firm among them. "So long as we are alive and steady, you need not fear. The Daityas will not be able to do anything to us." Then he turned to the bewildered Prabhavati. "Your father, your uncles, your brothers and your kinsmen are waiting with clubs in their hands. For your sake they deserve our respect and honour — but the time is dreadful. If we endure this, we shall die; if we fight, we shall succeed. Consult with your two sisters, and tell us what we should do, for we are under your orders."

Prabhavati knelt, her hands on her forehead, weeping. "Take up your arms and protect yourself. If you survive, you will see your wife and your sons. Remember the honourable Rukmini and Aniruddha, and save yourself from this peril. A great rishi conferred a boon on me: that I would lead a blameless life forever, never be a widow, and my sons would live. I have hope that his words will not be falsified." She rinsed her mouth, and placed a sword in her husband's hands.

Beyond the city, the armies of Vajranabha were gathering for the march on heaven. Within it, a woman who carried a rishi's promise armed her husband for the war that would test whether that promise would hold.
reflection: Kashyapa's warning is not a threat but an account of how sovereignty actually works: Indra rules because he serves the well-being of all creatures, not because he is the strongest. Vajranabha hears only the prophecy of death and marches toward it. Set against his pride is Prabhavati, a daughter of the enemy who arms her Yadava husband on the strength of a rishi's word — boon against boon, promise against promise.
next_story_tease: Meanwhile Dwaraka was preparing a different kind of return — one that would bring the parijata tree and the captive maidens of Naraka's house back to Krishna's city.
